articles.title: SubSea Craft Unveils Modular Payload Cassettes for MARS USV
articles.text:
SubSea Craft (SSC) has unveiled a new modular payload cassette system for MARS, their compact Unmanned Surface Vessel (USV), enabling the delivery of mission-configurable effects in contested environments.

SubSea Craft press release

Designed for expeditionary operations, the new patent-pending system uses dedicated cassettes which can be installed, removed and exchanged by a two-person team whilst deployed. This allows MARS to be quickly reconfigured for different missions, reducing integration timelines and accelerating the introduction of new payloads.

The cassette system has been informed by end user engagement, supporting MARS’ ability to adapt to evolving operational requirements while maintaining a simple and deployable operating concept.

Potential payload cassettes include loitering munitions, miniature torpedoes, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), sonobuoys and other mission-specific equipment, all delivered from the same core platform.

The payload cassette system has already supported the successful integration of the Anduril ALTIUS loitering munition, demonstrating MARS’ ability to rapidly integrate and deploy new effectors through a simple cassette exchange without modification to the vessel itself.

Tom Harkin, Chief Commercial Officer, said:

“We’ve designed the cassette system to make payload integration as simple as possible. Rather than making changes to the vessel every time a new payload is introduced, operators can swap cassettes quickly and easily. It gives MARS the flexibility to evolve as mission requirements change while keeping the platform itself unchanged.

The ability to rapidly integrate and deploy new payloads and effectors is becoming increasingly important. The cassette system supports that approach and gives users far greater flexibility in how they configure and employ MARS.”

articles.title: Microsoft to bounce mail from outdated Exchange servers
articles.text: Microsoft is upping the ante on Exchange Server security, warning that outdated on-premises systems will soon be blocked from sending email to Exchange Online. From the second week of September, Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 machines that send email to Exchange Online through an inbound connector of the OnPremises type must be patched to the final public update baseline released in October 2025, according to Microsoft. "This update level was released almost a year ago," Microsoft stated, "and all organizations should have updated to it." Microsoft has been advancing its "oldest acceptable version" for some time, but this change takes the baseline to the final public update for Exchange 2016 and 2019. Any subsequent increase would leave only customers enrolled in the Extended Security Update (ESU) program or those who have migrated to Exchange Server Subscription Edition able to meet it. Organizations may retain on-premises Exchange servers to support hybrid deployments, applications, or other systems that depend on them for email. According to Microsoft, throttling and blocking apply only to servers sending email to Exchange Online through an inbound OnPremises connector. Other delivery methods are unaffected, and the policy does not necessarily cover "all servers in your organization." The company added: "This might change in the future," which doesn't sound sinister at all. Administrators must balance the need to apply security patches promptly against the risk that an update introduces problems of its own – something Microsoft has, to put it delicately, caused in the past. Some administrators responding to the announcement were more than a little perturbed, although Microsoft has applied throttling and blocking to "significantly out of date" Exchange Server installations for several years. The announcement gives administrators advance notice of a change Microsoft says would have happened anyway. "With or without this announcement, the change would have been made (just as it was made in the past, without any announcement)," explained Microsoft Principal Project Manager Nino Bilic. "The bottom line is that admins really need to understand that updating Exchange should be done on time." ®

articles.title: PostgreSQL 19 connects the dots with standardized graph queries
articles.text: PostgreSQL 19 is set to add standardized SQL syntax for querying property graphs. The open source database has steadily grown in popularity over the last five years, becoming the most popular among developers for the first time in 2023. Speaking to The Register, Alastair Turner, PostgreSQL evangelist at open source consultancy Percona, said the property graph query support in PostgreSQL 19 – due later this month or early October – resulted from collaboration among several of the database's largest contributors. Graph databases store data as nodes, relationships, and properties rather than tables or documents. They have advantages for certain workloads, but adopting one can mean adding another DBMS to the technology stack. The relational database has been acquiring graph query capabilities for some time, but PostgreSQL 19 is set to go further, Turner explained. "All the rest of it has sort of been done through Object Relational Mapping over the top. This is actually baked-in graph syntax. It comes from the SQL 2023 standard." Turner said the implementation was "very heavily influenced" by some of the engineers behind OpenCypher, the open source query language for graph databases. The work also involved PostgreSQL committers who sit on the SQL standards committee. "This is one of the most interesting developments because it's one of the big multi-vendor collaborations. There was lots of coding and review work across quite a few of the big contributors," he said. The new capability implements SQL/PGQ, which became part of the SQL standard in 2023. "It's on the right path," Turner said. "The SQL community and the PostgreSQL community are going to try to optimize everything." However, he added that the implementation "still needs one or two additional syntax features" before it can displace dedicated graph databases for a significant number of workloads. Turner said: "The current implementation creates queries across node-edge graphs to satisfy those requests. So some of them perform very well. What's going to have to happen in the next iteration or two is that indexing add-ons catch up to improve the performance." ®

articles.title: ADA is on Engineer Hiring Spear to Strengthen AMCA and Tejas Mk2 Development
articles.text:
The Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) has opened a huge recruitment drive for 111 Project Assistant-1 posts, which could see a significant number of young engineers enter the fray for India’s fighter-aircraft development ecosystem. The Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) is responsible for design and development of programmes including the LCA Tejas, LCA Mk2 and Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA).
The latest recruitment is seeking engineers and technical graduates across disciplines relevant to advanced aerospace development. The ADA has traditionally used the Project Assistant-1 route to bring engineers into aeronautical and aerospace engineering, mechanical engineering, electronics and communication, computer science and related disciplines, with GATE-qualified and postgraduate candidates being important parts of the talent pool.
ADA is currently grappling with two very challenging programmes, Tejas Mk2 and AMCA, requiring extensive work on aerodynamics, structures, avionics, systems integration and certification. The notification does not specify if these 111 posts are allocated to either of these two programmes, However, the sheer scale of the recruitment drive is difficult to ignore, as it fits in well with the workload that ADA has currently on its plate regarding multiple Combat aircraft programs in the country.
ADA being only nodal design agency in the country it is increasingly reliant now on computational design and analysis prior to any hardware being produced. Work on CFD, finite-element analysis, structural optimization and software-in-the-loop testing can identify potential showstoppers prior to them rearing their ugly heads on a test bed.
This is especially crucial for further optimtization in AMCA as stealth shaping, internal weapons bays, twin-engined propulsion and weight-reduction measures have to be balanced out in concert. Every single kg cut down from the airframe has direct impact on the aircraft’s fuel fraction, payload capacity and range, and therefore this cannot be a one-time effort but an ongoing process. More manpower would allow ADA’s aerodynamics, structures, propulsion and software divisions to work in parallel on various aspects of the design rather than sequentially. This could make a significant difference to the projected timeline.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

articles.title: Indian Army remains mum on INSAS Retirement Plans, after Ak-203 intake increases
articles.text:
Indian Army has not confirmed till when it plans to retire its INSAS rifle from its fleet even though Made in India Ak-203 Assault Rifle deliveries have picked up in last few years and now nearly 100 percent of the AK-203 is Made in the country without any supplied from Russian Side.
INSAS has been the standard issue rifle of the Indian Army since late 90s, replacing the old SLR family. The Indian Army alone is estimated to have between 7.6 to 10 lakh INSAS rifles, constituting the majority of a roughly 8.1 lakh strong assault rifle inventory of the three services. Add to that more than two decades of concurrent service in the Central Armed Police Forces as well as the state police forces, and it becomes obvious as to why replacing this rifle would not exactly be a cakewalk. Few weapon systems in the world are replaced at this scale in such a short span of time.
Indian Army is carrying out phase procurement of two assault rifles that will eventually replace all INSAS Rifles , It has procured SIG-716 chambered in 7.62x51mm has been inducted in thousands of units already. In 2024, an additional order for 72,000 SIG716 assault rifles was signed in addition to the initial contract for 72,400 rifles acquired in 2019. The procurement targets at filling up the frontline infantry need vis-a-vis China and Pakistan. Further, the Indian Army has also laid out plans to procure the AK-203 assault rifles as part of the 6.01 lakh rifle acquisition plan. The rifles are produced by the Indo-Russia Rifles joint venture, located at Korwa in Amethi.
It is estimated that between 500,000 and 700,000 INSAS rifles are still in service by the Indian Armed Forces, the greater part being in the possession of the Indian Army. Although more than 900,000 INSAS rifles (Indian Small Arms System) have been produced since its introduction in 1998, the weapon is at the end of a massive phased-out retirement on multiple fronts.
idrw.org was told by Indian Army official that amount of guns cant be replaced in short time and will continue to be used for better half into next decade also as some of them will be kept as reserves and some will be transferred to Paramilitary forces or local state Police based on their requirements, but he did agree that some might be scrapped that have sustained damages or were used as spares for other guns.
While Indian Army is not only one that doesnt want to operate INSAS anymore as seen of late even ITBP has opted to go for the AK-203, arguing that because they are going to be posted in sensitive areas in conjunction with the Army, and both are likely to share supplies of common ammunition, it made sense to have a weapon system that could be used by both.
The BSF, on its part, is looking at DRDO’s indigenous Ugram rifle as a possible successor to INSAS, which is also a product of private partner Dvipa Armour, offers a 500 metre range with a weapon that weighs under 4 kg. The CAPFs have around 10 lakh personnel apart from the 14 lakh sanctioned for the Army, so the actual impact of this change across all of India’s uniformed forces is substantially bigger than suggested by the Army figures.
It not be immediate end of INSAS in Army but sure its days are numbered.

articles.title: DRDO advances work on 155mm Ramjet Projectile with 80 km Range, that Could Transform Indian Army Artillery
articles.text:
India is developing a new 155mm ramjet-powered artillery projectile to substantially enhance the range of conventional tube artillery. A display from the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) shows the configuration and performance target of the indigenous munition, which will enable Indian Army artillery units to strike deep into enemy territory without the use of expensive long-range missiles.
The projectile displayed by DRDO is named 155mm Ramjet Projectile and its stated aim is to develop ramjet projectile technology for artillery guns. The displayed specifications state a target range of at least 80 km, a projectile mass of approximately 48 kg, a high-explosive payload exceeding 3.5 kg, muzzle velocity of at least 875 m/s, and an indicated specific impulse (ISP) of more than 900 s.
DRDO has previously displayed the technology publicly, including at Aero India 2025, where it displayed a 155mm ramjet projectile for the 155mm/52-calibre Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System (ATAGS). DRDO told Janes at the event that the technology was still being established and that the projectile would extend the range of ATAGS to as much as 80 km, compared with around 45 km using existing ammunition.
The concept represents a major leap from conventional artillery ammunition. A traditional artillery shell derives most of its kinetic energy from the gun during launch and subsequently follows a ballistic trajectory. A ramjet projectile, by contrast, uses an air-breathing propulsion system after launch. The high velocity generated by the gun allows air to enter the projectile’s intake, where it supports combustion and generates additional thrust during flight.
The displayed design incorporates a front intake ramjet motor, a fuel-right propellant, a propulsion and propellant system, and a consumer charger section. The projectile also features wrap-around fins for in-flight stability, a slipping driving band and a disposable rear cap.
The use of a front-mounted air intake is particularly important as the projectile has to function within the extreme aerodynamic and thermal environment created immediately after being fired from a large-calibre artillery weapon. It has to survive the enormous acceleration and stresses associated with gun launch and subsequently function as an air-breathing propulsion system.
India’s research into this technology has been ongoing for several years. Researchers at IIT Madras have worked on developing fuel-rich solid propellants specific to ramjet-powered 155mm artillery applications. A Defence Science Journal paper showed research into fuel-rich propellants intended to provide active propulsion to a 155mm artillery shell and examined the ballistic and combustion characteristics required for the application.
The technology could provide the Indian Army with a valuable middle ground between conventional artillery and tactical missiles. An 80-km-class artillery projectile would enable gun units to attack command posts, radar installations, surveillance equipment, forward operating locations and other high-value targets substantially deeper than is possible with standard ammunition.
The DRDO display specifically lists roles including striking targets deep inside enemy territory, neutralising or destroying critical areas economically, and engaging targets such as radars, surveillance equipment, command posts and forward operating locations.
This is significant as artillery remains significantly cheaper and more scalable than missile systems for many battlefield missions. A ramjet projectile could deliver extended-range effects while maintaining the logistical benefits of artillery ammunition and using existing 155mm gun infrastructure.
DRDO’s May 2025 newsletter also confirmed that its Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE) was brief visitors on the 155mm Ramjet Projectile, alongside programmes such as ATAGS, Pinaka and 155mm ammunition.
The technology is also part of a broader effort to enhance the effectiveness of India’s 155mm artillery fleet. The Army has a diverse family of 155mm systems, including ATAGS, M777, Dhanush, Sharang and K9 Vajra, creating a potentially large user base for advanced ammunition if the projectile actually achieves the required levels of reliability, accuracy, safety, and production maturity.
One of the most important features shown on the DRDO display is miniaturised guidance and navigation capability, with the specification stating accuracy of 10 metres or better with GNC. If achieved operationally, such precision would make the ramjet projectile substantially more useful against point and area targets than an unguided extended-range shell.
The 155mm ramjet projectile therefore represents more than just a longer-range artillery round. It is an attempt to combine gun-launched acceleration, air-breathing propulsion, guidance and conventional artillery logistics into a single weapon.
For the Indian Army, successful development of the system would provide a cost-effective long-range strike option and alleviate the burden on missile inventories for targets that can be serviced by artillery.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

articles.title: Virupaksha AESA Radar: How India’s Su-30MKI Radar Upgrade Could Improve Detection of Chinese J-20 Fleet
articles.text:
India’s Virupaksha active electronically scanned array radar, being developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s Electronics and Radar Development Establishment for the Indian Air Force’s Su-30MKI upgrade, is one of the most ambitious indigenous airborne-radar programmes undertaken for the fighter jet type in India. The radar is set to replace the Su-30MKI’s Russian-origin N011M Bars radar that was a Hybrid PESA system but now its dated as tech was from late 80s.
Virupaksha radar will have approximately 950-mm antenna aperture and approximately 2,400 transmit/receive (TR) modules, according to DRDO officials when the radar was unveiled at Aero India 2025. The radar employs gallium-nitride (GaN) TR modules which offer greater power-handling capability, improved thermal characteristics and wider-band performance than older GaAs-based architectures.
The large array density is particularly significant to the Su-30MKI as it possesses a comparatively large nose to accommodate a substantial radar aperture. Rather than replacing Bars with just another mechanically-scanned radar system, Virupaksha is set to be a modern multifunction AESA radar, capable of supporting several simultaneous functions.
The radar is set to be a 4D radar, able to determine the target range, azimuth, elevation and relative velocity. Its modes include air-to-air, close-combat, air-to-ground, air-to-sea and navigation functions. It is also designed with electronic counter-countermeasure capabilities for use in a contested electromagnetic environment.
Its relevance against stealth aircraft such as China’s J-20 needs more careful consideration. It would be misleading to give a specific detection range again any stealth aircraft such as the J-20 without having classified information on the radar’s operating frequency, waveform, processing gain, array efficiency, transmitted power and the aircraft’s radar cross-section. DRDO has not publicly disclosed any of these parameters of Virupaksha.
What can be said with greater confidence is that the radar’s large aperture, GaN technology, advanced processing and ECCM architecture should considerably improve the Su-30MKI’s ability to detect and track difficult targets, compared to its legacy Bars radar. However, detection of any low-observable aircraft is not simply a matter of increasing the power of the transmitter.
Stealth reduces the strength of the radar return available to the receiver, while the actual engagements depend upon aspects such as the aspect angle, frequency, atmospheric conditions, electronic warfare, target manoeuvring and the performance of both aircraft’s sensors. A large and powerful AESA can improve the detection equation, but cannot negate the fundamental advantages offered by a low-observable airframe.
The radar’s wide field of regard is another potentially important feature. According to reports, the radar is mounted on a repositioning mechanism, which expands the angular coverage beyond that which could be achieved by a conventional fixed forward-facing AESA. The concept is particularly useful for a large fighter such as the Su-30MKI as it can allow the aircraft to keep sensor coverage while manoeuvring away from the target axis. However, the exact operational field-of-regard figures must be treated with caution, until officially confirmed.
The radar will also be more valuable when integrated with the Su-30MKI’s wider sensor and weapons architecture. An AESA radar, infrared search-and-track system, electronic-warfare suite, helmet-mounted display, datalink and long-range air-to-air missiles can collectively provide a much stronger BVR engagement capability than any individual subsystem.
This is particularly relevant to the Super Sukhoi programme. The objective is not simply to install a new radar, but to transform the Su-30MKI into a considerably more capable networked 4.5 + gen combat aircraft.

The tokamak (an acronym from the Russian words for toroidal magnetic confinement) was developed in the mid-1960s by Soviet plasma physicists. It produces the highest plasma temperatures, densities, and confinement durations of any confinement device.

articles.title: Pakistan Panics over major Air Exercises in Western Sector by India
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) is set for two consecutive air exercises in the western sector next month, and from across the border in Islamabad, it is seen as a serious matter. A long NOTAM for the activity in the Jodhpur sector has already been raised in defense circles, indicating that something important is on the horizon.
The first of the two exercises to be held at the AFJodhpur airbase is Veer Guardian 26, the second edition of the bilateral India-Japan air-to-air combat training exercise, which is scheduled to be held from September 9 to 21. It marks the first time that Japan Air Self-Defence Force fighters will participate on Indian territory. Three F-2A jets of the 8th Air Wing based at Tsuiki, along with approximately 110 personnel, are expected to travel a long distance through Okinawa and Thailand, with the USAF providing aerial refueling support en route.
It will hardly be over before the larger one is launched: Tarang Shakti 2026 IAF’s premier multi-national exercise, which is slated to be held at the Jodhpur airbase from September 26 to October 12, is expected to see the participation of around eight countries. There are rumors that the American F-35 stealth fighter jet is going to make its debut appearance on the territory of India for drills.
Pakistani Defence minister Khawaja Asif was seen in media commenting that ” we are monitoring the situation and will respond if India tries to do something in disguise of air exercises”
Jodhpur is located near the international border and is one of the IAF’s most critical bases facing the western neighbor. It was the location of the IAF’s combat operations during the 1965 and 1971 wars. Hosting a Japanese fighter deployment and then, several weeks later, a fifth-generation American jet at the same base practically on the doorstep of Pakistan is sure to be viewed in Islamabad as more than just routine training.
For observers of the western front, there are a few things to keep an eye out for. Whether or not the F-35 participation materializes, given the technological sensitivity close to the border, will certainly be of interest. So will be how the Pakistan Air Force reacts operationally, if at all, to counter-deployments or public statements.

articles.title: ‘Eye in sky’: ISRO launches advanced earth observation satellite for ‘strategic data’
articles.text:
ISRO on Friday made its way into history books yet again with the successful launch of the country’s first ever imaging satellite in geo-orbit, placing the over 2,300 kg payload into a precise orbit using a GSLV rocket. Friday’s launch marked the space agency’s maiden success for the year 2026.
The EOS-05 satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit, about 18 minutes after it lifted off from the spaceport here, ISRO announced.
While several earth observation satellites operate from low earth orbit (LEO), the EOS-5 satellite is set to hover at an altitude of roughly 36,000 km above earth, which is the geosynchronous orbit and at that level, the satellite will match Earth’s rotational speed.
At over 2,300 kg, this is the heaviest satellite ever to be carried by a GSLV and the satellite was perfectly ahead in its trajectory.
“The eye in the sky,” as one of the senior scientists involved in the mission described the satellite, is set to provide real-time imagery and help the nation in areas including agriculture, and disaster management.
The mission success, following some earlier failures, was apparently a morale booster.A beaming ISRO chief V Narayanan said: “I am very happy to announce that the GSLV F-17 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the advanced EOS-05 geo imaging satellite in the intended and required orbit.”
“This is the 107th launch from Srihariharikota and the 19th mission of GSLV,” the Secretary, Department of Space, flanked by key scientists involved in the mission, said soon after the launch.He recalled that the first launch of GSLV (D1) was done with a payload of 1,536 kg and since then, gradually, ISRO improved the performance of GSLV by optimising the structural mass, and improving the propulsion systems. “Today, we have injected the heaviest satellite 2,367 kg using this launch vehicle.”
Once the EOS-05 is operationalised in the orbit, it will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo-orbit providing “strategic data” for the country, he said.
Quoting satellite data, he confirmed that all the systems were operating perfectly well and that the solar panel has been successfully deployed. “The health of satellite is perfectly alright,” he said.
“This is a great achievement for our country’s space programme because this is the first EOS that will be placed on the geo platform for the national activities.”
In the days to come, the orbit raising maneuvering will be done and the satellite will be elevated to required orbit and will be placed in the geo platform, he said, adding the success is the culmination of team work of ISRO and its industrial partners. Mission Director Thomas Kurien said the mission carried uniquely configured EOS capable of near real time imaging. “It is the heaviest satellite ever launched by GSLV into a GTO or sub-GTO orbit,” he added.Project Director (Satellite) Imteyaz Ahamad described the EOS-05 as a unique, one of its kind satellite with multi-band operating capabilities. “It is a complex satellite in terms of configuration, content and capability.”
Earlier, at the end of a smooth 27-hour countdown, which commenced at 23.30 hours on Wednesday, the rocket began its ascent on dot at 2.55 AM from the second launch pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre. The odd hour and rain could not deter the enthusiasm of members of public as many, armed with umbrellas, turned up in good numbers to cheer the launch.
The 3-stage, 51.7 meter Geosynchronous Launch Vehicle (GSLV), with its third stage being cryogenic, has a lift off mass of 420.5 tonne and the heavy satellite is ensconced on the rocket nose cone.
The GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission is said to be a replacement for the unsuccessful GSLV-F-10/EOS-03 mission of 2021.An onboard computer had aborted that mission at 307 seconds into the flight then. A probe into the post-flight data had indicated that an anomaly in the Cryogenic Upper Stage led to the mission failure, according to ISRO.
The pre-dawn launch on Friday follows a gap of nearly eight months and brings ISRO its first success of the year.On January 12, ISRO’s PSLV-C62 rocket carrying 16 satellites failed to place them in the intended orbit after encountering an “anomaly” in the critical third stage of the launch.
Days ago, ISRO chairman V Narayanan visited the Tirumala Tirupati Lord Venkateshwara Swamy temple and prayed for the mission’s success.

articles.title: India, Belgium decide to expand defence ties
articles.text:
India and Belgium on Thursday inked several pacts to shore up their defence ties including to facilitate joint manufacturing of military hardware in line with the broader aim to further bolster their strategic partnership.
The decision to expand the defence ties was taken during talks between Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and his Belgian counterpart Theo Francken. The defence ministerial dialogue was held ahead of wide-ranging discussions between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Belgian counterpart Bart De Wever.
The Singh-Francken talks saw both sides reviewing the entire spectrum of defence and industrial cooperation and agreeing to expand the engagement through training and capacity building initiatives.
“Both leaders also discussed issues of regional peace and security and acknowledged the need for maritime security collaboration in the Indo-Pacific. They reiterated that the partnership between India and Belgium is based on shared values of mutual trust and respect,” the defence ministry said. Following the meeting between Modi and De Wever, the two sides inked a defence framework pact. Separately, 10 agreements on collaboration between Belgian and Indian defence industries were signed, involving production of Belgian military hardware such as rockets in India.
“India is a rapidly growing economy and a major military power in the Indo-Pacific. The country is also strategically located along some of the world’s most important trade routes,” Francken said.
“For an open trading nation like Belgium, the security of these sea lanes is vital. At the same time, Europe’s security is increasingly interconnected with developments in Asia,” he said.
Francken also flagged concerns over Russia’s war in Ukraine and its cooperation with Iran and North Korea in the military sphere.
“China is becoming increasingly assertive in the Indo-Pacific. What happens in Asia has consequences for Europe. And vice versa. Our security does not stop at our borders. articles.title: JavaScript installer pnpm recast in Rust because ECMAScript can't keep up
articles.text: The popular JavaScript package manager pnpm, already known for its speedy downloads, has further cut installation times by up to 90 percent thanks to a complete rewrite in Rust. Yet the freshly released version 12 of pnpm should not cause consternation while upgrading, its maintainer says. “Upgrading should not feel like a migration. The commands, flags, settings, and lockfile format of pnpm 11 all carry over, and the documentation covers both versions,” wrote Zoltan Kochan, the current lead maintainer of pnpm. In the project’s own benchmarks, pnpm 12 installed a sample uncached package in 5.19 seconds, compared to the 8.22 seconds pnpm 11 required and the 47.7 seconds npm itself required. The project team also built a registry server in Rust, called pnpr, which improves performance even further. In the above test, the installation took only 3.37 seconds with pnpr on the backend. A new Rust core binary, on which work started in April, eliminates a lot of the overhead that comes from routing filesystem work through Node.js. This new version is 65.9 percent Rust and 33.5 percent TypeScript, according to the GitHub stats. “Package installation is dominated by fetching metadata and tarballs, unpacking files, resolving dependency graphs, and linking packages into node_modules, making it a natural target for native code and parallelism,” wrote Sarah Gooding, vice president of communications for security provider Socket, in a blog post. Gooding also noted that the project benchmarked pnpm against Bun and Yarn, but the results were removed due to testing SNAFUs. Nonetheless, she noted the software cut install times by up to 90 percent in some cases. A faster npm Developer Rico Sta. Cruz originally created pnpm in 2016 as a faster alternative to npm (Node Package Manager), JavaScript’s de facto package manager, which devs used to find and download libraries and tools. GitHub acquired the open source npm software and repository in 2020. Npm garnered a reputation for being both sluggish and hungry for disk space, thanks to its generous practice of downloading all needed dependencies onto users’ machines, regardless of whether they were duplicates. Pnpm’s secret sauce is content-addressable storage. If you need a single library for 100 different applications, pnpm downloads it only once, and downloads another copy only if the developer specifies a different version. Like npm, pnpm still draws from the official npm repository, but arguably works better than npm for many. Many devs also like that the lockfile describing the package’s dependency tree was more readable thanks to its use of YAML. The 2025 State of JavaScript survey showed that pnpm was by far the most popular package manager for JavaScript monorepos, a party that also included Nx, Lerna, Yalc, Turborepo and even npm’s built-in Workspaces. About 38 percent (3,840) of 10,251 surveyed developers used the package manager. Rust for JavaScript Rewriting applications in Rust seems to be a favorite activity these days, as the language is known for speedy performance unhampered by garbage collection. In the Web app ecosystem alone, the Bun framework just got an AI-fueled Rust makeover, Tailwind CSS version 4 got a new Rust engine called Oxide, and the Vite framework now speeds along thanks to a Rust-built JavaScript bundler called Rolldown. “It is a bit of [an] indictment on Node for having poor dx” (developer experience), wrote Darcy Clarke, CEO of JavaScript package management platform provider vlt, in an X message, about the Rust rewrite of pnpm. “It was faster to rewrite pnpm in rust than to migrate to esm” (ECMAScript modules), replied pnpm's Kochan, agreeing with Clarke’s sentiment. The software’s GitHub page still points at the last major release, pnpm 11.25, so existing users will have to update to the v12 branch specifically (“pnpm self-update next-12” will get you there). ®

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace

—Cory Alpert, a researcher at the University of Melbourne studying AI’s impact on democracy, who previously served in the Biden White House.

Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones. But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector: the data those drones generate.

Ukraine has begun making millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to military contractors and commercial companies. It’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships, but it turns the front line into a model training site, using the chaos of war to create conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce.

As this new industry takes shape, we need a regulatory system that ensures battlefield data isn’t treated like ordinary commercial material.

Read the full op-ed on why battlefield data needs new rules.

Mother tongue

—“Mother Tongue” is a short fiction story by author and AI ethicist Jenny Williams

“Daddy?” Theo curled against my side in bed. “Where do words go when they die?

“Well, kiddo,” I said, scratching my beard. “Words aren’t really alive to begin with. Not like you and I are alive.”

Inside, Theo’s AI companion teaches him strange songs in a language his father doesn’t understand. But outside, the world is edging toward disaster. A mysterious agentic system called Tingsu has emerged in a nuclear-armed country, and no one seems to understand what it wants.

These days, Google, Samsung, and Apple support phones with software updates for the better part of a decade, but will the hardware last that long? And what happens when it needs a repair? You may be out of luck or out a lot of money, but Fairphone prioritizes the self-repair experience.

However, at a launch event on Thursday, Wayve showed off the follow-up to the Mustang: a Nissan LEAF, which will run the Wayve AI Driver using NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion. Unlike the Mustang, the LEAF's self-driving equipment looked as though it might have been part of the car's design, from a roof-mounted sensor pack that followed the roofline, through to sensors attached to the wings and bumpers. Right now, Uber stated, "The initial launch phase features supervised autonomous rides, meaning a trained and TfL licensed private hire driver is onboard to oversee the trip." So no San Francisco Waymo-esque rides with the driver's seat spookily empty just yet. However, a Wayve representative told us the Nissan LEAF would eventually be capable of such a feat. The rollout of the Mustang feels a little like a stunt to steal a march on competitors such as Waymo, which has also had vehicles rolling around the tricky streets and traffic of London. Waymo is presently in a testing phase, but Wayve and Uber are now taking paying passengers. Both services, however, must have a trained driver onboard, poised to intervene if the need arises. The untried nature of the Wayve and Uber Mustang is evidenced by the words "TEST VEHICLE. KEEP A SAFE DISTANCE" printed on the rear of the car. Paying passengers are part of the AI Driver's learning process, with lessons learned feeding into the next generation of autonomous vehicles, which might, or might not, still need that safety driver behind the wheel, just in case. Data from drones in Ukraine is fueling a new Wild West marketplace
articles.text:
Battlefields in Ukraine are littered with the remnants of drones, which are now firmly established as a critical weapon of modern warfare. But behind all that wreckage, there’s a new gold mine for the defense sector. The data drones generate will far outlast the wars in which they are used to fight, increasingly becoming part of the AI architecture that shapes even civilian life.  

For every flight, unmanned systems collect thousands of points of data, from images and video to controller inputs. Together, those records show how a machine and a person responded to constantly shifting circumstances. 

Ukraine has now begun converting that experience into a resource. Its Ministry of Defense announced in January that it would make millions of data points gathered during tens of thousands of drone flights available to both military contractors and commercial companies, and since then more than 100 companies and the UK government have gained access.

For a country at war, it’s a quick way to attract funding and partnerships. But this step turns the front line into an active site of model training, taking advantage of how the chaos of war creates conditions that AI companies struggle to reproduce on their own.

Other countries and battlefields are likely to follow Ukraine’s lead, but the responsibility for governing this new industry cannot fall solely on a country fighting for its survival. That legal vacuum has to be filled together by the countries and companies involved in this industry’s development.  

Explosive growth

Ukraine’s battlefields are not the first to produce records used to train and develop models: American drones over Syria and Yemen collected data that informed the first generation of semiautonomous military hardware in the late 2010s.

The difference now is that access to that data is being used to develop a wider ecosystem. And the financial value to defense firms is immense: Battlefield data offers large volumes of machine experience gathered under conditions that no laboratory can produce.

That’s because the data that’s most valuable for training AI models comes from exceptions: the moment visibility disappears, a signal jams, or a human operator improvises. AI companies spend years and enormous sums trying to capture enough of these moments to make their models more robust. But war produces them at a frequency controlled testing cannot match.

This constantly changing terrain is what makes drone data valuable far beyond the battlefield. A commercial drone used for delivery or remote sensing may never encounter artillery fire, but it must still operate with incomplete information in a world where people behave unpredictably. The same problem is compressed by war into a much shorter timeline. 

Processed and matched against records of what its operator was doing, that data turns operational records into training sets. Combat becomes a commercial asset.

Many conflicts have already seen this training loop happen as drone footage feeds subsequent generations of military technology, and the market is set to grow. Enabled Intelligence, an American company that specializes in processing data to become usable in AI training, says it has already made more than half a million hours of Ukrainian drone footage available to feed into the next round of models, advertising possible uses in both military and commercial systems.

Closing the data loop

Many of the drones that now define our modern age of warfare began as civilian technology. But they’ve recently been turbocharged by new, commercially available AI systems, which allow cheap machines to operate autonomously—either individually or as a flock—as the environment changes around them. Each flight then creates a record of what the system encountered.

The resulting data is critical. The controlled lab environments usually developed to train these autonomous systems can approximate failure but are no match for  the live conditions of a battlefield with very real risks. Military intelligence programs have held data generated by sensor-heavy systems like Predator and Reaper drones for nearly a decade through programs like Project Maven, but access remained entirely within the defense world. The data generated was available only through restricted, classified channels for the sole purpose of developing new weapons systems that would feed back into the same military that produced the data in the first place. That experience is now being shared to a much broader development network. 

The loop now closes. Commercial technologies adapted for the battlefield are generating data that can flow back into the industries from which they came, becoming part of the data infrastructure relied on by governments and the private sector alike. 

Drones that were trained in the signal-jammed airspace over Ukraine are now being deployed in the agricultural sector to help farmers map and survey their fields in places lacking the cell signal necessary for previous generations of technology. 

Other countries are likely to follow Ukraine in selling their battlefield data, and we are not ready for the new marketplace this will create.

Bad actors could acquire the data, but purchase controls already mitigate that risk. Intelligence operatives scrutinize potential customers’ infrastructure for ways that data could reach enemies or nefarious actors. 

Training data creates a new tracing problem, though. Whereas the movement of commercial datasets can be followed when planted contact details appear two steps from the original buyer, the provenance of AI training data vanishes in a manner embedded in the technology itself. Another risk is that this use of the data creates an extractive economy in which wealthier countries far from danger benefit from the mortal threat borne by frontline states, potentially creating a market incentive for war to continue as an unending mine for digital gold. 

A fraught new frontier

Existing laws regulate how militaries may conduct war. But they say almost nothing about what happens when records created in combat are stripped of their operational context, packaged as data, and licensed to companies whose products circulate far beyond where they were made.

The responsibilities of the companies that design these systems remain unsettled. Ukraine is building access controls, which are mentioned in the newly signed UK-Ukraine AI agreement, but no governments are actively working on regulating what happens when data has been absorbed into a model and crosses back into civilian markets.

Those records contain human lives. The soldiers and civilians visible in them did not agree to become training material for products that might be sold years later. But sensor data, camera footage, and coordinates from civilians fleeing a drone strike now constitute the sorts of data that inform how future machines will make decisions.

That is a problem of consent. Individuals featured in the data—be they targets, controllers, or civilians standing by—become part of the training material. The autonomous capabilities based on that data do not stop at the edge of the battlefield. Such capabilities move into other military or commercial systems like delivery vehicles or agricultural machinery. Errors and assumptions embedded in the data travel with the model even once it enters civilian life.

Battlefield data should not be treated as ordinary commercial material. But there is currently no agency or regulator that has jurisdiction over this issue. In the meantime, governments that provide access to defense data should treat it as they would a controlled weapons transfer, recording its origin, licensing its users, and restricting onward sharing. Ukraine has begun to grapple with this. Its Avengers Labs program allows companies to train models on battlefield data without giving them direct access to sensitive databases. Yet that mitigates only one part of the problem. 

Governments should require disclosure when models trained on wartime material are later incorporated into civilian products. The goal of such regulation should be to make the path from combat to commerce visible. 

What these companies are really mining is experience. And soldiers cannot consent to having their experience used in this way—as training data that produces model advantage and ultimately supports a product used far from where the war was fought.

The question is no longer only what the technology companies can sell for use in war. It is what they can extract from it.

To protect ourselves from the excesses of this new industry, we need a regulatory system that follows battlefield data wherever it goes, from combat to model to commercial product. 

Cory Alpert is a researcher at the University of Melbourne, looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served in the Biden White House.

articles.title: US law firm accuses UK AI software firm of unwanted contract renewal when it tried to leave
articles.text: A US law firm is alleging that UK-based telecoms and software company ConnexAI sold it software and AI systems that failed to perform as the vendor claimed, and then unlawfully renewed its contract. ConnexAI has rejected the allegations. The dispute has involves two court cases, both of which are ongoing. DK Law, a personal injury specialist based in California, alleged in a California court filing in April that ConnexAI promises “customers a telephone system and AI software solution with functionality that does not exist or perform as represented.” It also alleges in the California complaint [PDF] that ConnexAI continued to send it invoices after it had told the vendor it was not renewing the year-long contract. The Register understands that ConnexAI believes the allegations to be frivolous and without merit. The vendor is branded ConnexAI, and registered as Connex One Limited in the UK and Connex One Inc in the US. The customer’s claim followed a complaint that ConnexAI itself filed against the law firm the month before. In March 2026, in a New York court, ConnexAI filed a complaint [PDF] claiming its law firm customer had breached its contract by failing to pay invoices. Dan Richardson, ConnexAI general manager of North America, said in a statement: “There is a limit to what we can say while the matter is before the court. This claim is one part of a wider dispute which was initiated by Connex One Inc. The allegations now being made are rejected, and we would note that they were raised only after we issued proceedings which are active.” In its complaint in the US District Court, Central District of California, Southern Division, DK Law alleges that ConnexAI sold it a telephone system and software on the basis that it would provide phone and voice services integrated with SMS and WhatsApp. ConnexAI also said its Athena software included “sentiment analysis, entity recognition, call transcripts, interaction clustering, training cues, and the ability to identify trends.” Crucially, it also claimed the AI transcription worked in Spanish. “ConnexAI represented that the Athena AI software included AI Agent, AI Guru, AI Analytics, AI Voice, Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), all of which were represented to elevate customer interactions and enhance customer engagement and experience,” the filing said. Using AI agents would offer around-the-clock availability, faster response times and personalized interactions, with a “human-like voice and text-based communication,” the complaint argued. After less than a year using the software, DK Law alleged its experience of the software differed from the claims made by the vendor. According to the California filing, the telephone system frequently “went down”, with calls often dropped or unanswered. Calls were also consistently misrouted, the customer alleges. The problems were reported to the vendor’s support team. After the issue was escalated, the filing continues, ConnexAI sent US technical services engineers and the UK-based CTO to troubleshoot. “Sometimes the problem was resolved for the moment, only to recur shortly thereafter, with no permanent fix,” the complaint claimed. In addition, WhatsApp was unreliable and effectively unusable, DK Law alleges. While ConnexAI had claimed its ASR “would never miss a word,” DK Law claimed “this too was false.” Per the filing, on checking recordings of calls, the customer claims to have discovered that only a few seconds of a conversation were actually recorded despite evidence of a longer call. “Connex also represented in pre-contract discussions that its software was able to create real-time call transcripts of customer interactions conducted in English and Spanish. However, in reality, the Connex software only sometimes produced a transcript. When compared to the recorded conversations, DK Law found the transcripts of calls conducted in English to be inaccurate, and the Spanish language transcription did not work at all,” the California law firm alleged. Given the performance, the filing claims, Brendan Haverlock, DK Law CTO, told the vendor that the contract would not be renewed after it expired in October 2025. But that was not the end of the matter. The complaint alleges ConnexAI continued to invoice DK Law after the end of the contract term, demanding payment and "harassing its employees" for payment, the customer alleged. In March 2026, Connex Inc, the US company, launched a legal claim in the New York case against DK Law in which it alleged DK Law had failed to make the required payments and breached its contract. The filing, which was originally made in the Supreme Court of the State of New York, and then moved to a New York District Court, said that in October 2024, the two companies entered into an agreement, which “renewed for a subsequent term commencing on October 8, 2025.” However, in the separate but related California filing in April, DK Law alleged that ConnexAI had already breached the contract “by failing… to implement and deliver telecommunications and software services in a manner consistent with industry standards.” It also said in the filing that ConnexAI's claim that the contract had automatically renewed was not in accordance with New York State law, which “required Connex to give written notice of the automatic renewal in advance.” The law covers telecommunications and software. ConnexAI “never provided the requisite notice of automatic renewal,” DK Law alleged. In the California Court, DK Law seeks restitution and damages. In a statement to The Register, ConnexAI’s Richardson questioned why Connex One Ltd was included on the California claim, given Connex Inc sued DK Law in New York. In the California filing, DK Law alleged the UK company “directly participated in the sales process, provided or controlled implementation and support personnel, and directed or ratified the post-notice renewal and retention conduct.” It said the US company is wholly owned and operated by the UK’s Connex One Limited and acted as a contracting arm or agent. The case is now waiting to move through the courts. Last week, (August 27) the California court denied DK Law’s claim, but only insofar as it “stayed” the case, pending the New York claim. In effect, that case is put on hold until the New York case is settled. DK Law is attempting to have the New York case dismissed and has requested the court hear oral arguments. On September 1, in an order and opinion filed by federal magistrate judge Katharine H Parker, the motion to stay the case was denied [PDF].® Reg note: We are not accepting comments on this article and have closed the forum.

articles.text: Britain's Ministry of Defence (MoD) is seeking anti-drone technology capable of protecting troops from saturation attacks designed to overwhelm defenses or exhaust their ammunition. The tender, dubbed Project PANOPTES, is being run by UK Defence Innovation (UKDI) on behalf of the MoD, with an initial £5 million ($6.8 million) available to successful bidders. First-stage submissions close at midday on September 23, suggesting that the MoD is in something of a hurry. According to the competition document, PANOPTES aims to deliver "an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System (C-UAS) force-protection capability, capable of autonomous operation." The MoD wants a system that complements its existing defenses by detecting, tracking, and defeating low-cost threats without being overwhelmed or rapidly exhausting its ammunition. It must operate autonomously and be mountable on an Army vehicle. UKDI is "particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors," although it will consider credible alternatives. The initial focus is on NATO Class 1 uncrewed aerial systems, a category covering military drones weighing up to 150 kg. These include the small battlefield craft used extensively in Ukraine against targets ranging from armored vehicles to individual soldiers, rather than larger drones intended to strike fixed installations. The requirement covers "single, repeated, sequential and simultaneous threat profiles" – including potential swarm attacks – as well as drones used for disruption or surveillance. Reg readers may recall that the British Army tested anti-drone laser systems a couple of years ago. Soldiers from 16 Royal Artillery fired a 15 kW infrared laser mounted on a Wolfhound armored truck against airborne targets, "neutralizing" them at distances beyond 1 km. The MoD told us at the time that those trials were merely a capability demonstration intended to improve its understanding of laser technology. PANOPTES appears to move closer to procuring an operational system, although it wouldn't be the first defense competition to lead nowhere. We asked the MoD for further details, including when it anticipates any successful solutions might make it into service with the British Army. PANOPTES has two stages: applicants first outline their ideas, after which those behind the most promising submissions will be invited to submit detailed proposals. Vulnerability to drones is a major concern for armed forces around the world. US defense startup Mara recently unveiled a counter-drone system that launches small interceptors from a vehicle roof, but these would eventually be used up in a battlefield situation. Britain's Royal Navy also put out a request for ship-based counter-drone systems earlier this year. Project TALON envisages combining kinetic projectiles with non-kinetic defenses such as lasers, microwaves, and electronic jamming. Royal Navy ships are already due to receive the DragonFire laser weapon, with the first system expected to be fitted to a Type 45 destroyer next year. Whether that technology can be shrunk or adapted for an Army vehicle is another matter. ®

articles.text: Comparing travel eSIM prices is not as simple as looking at a provider's homepage. Most companies advertise low starting prices, but what travelers actually pay depends on whether they can buy a plan that matches the length of their trip. If a provider only offers fixed duration packages, travelers may end up paying for several days of mobile data they do not need. For frequent travelers or longer trips, those extra days can quickly add to the total cost. The Travel eSIM Value Index 2026 compared three leading travel eSIM providers: Holafly, Saily and Airalo. The ranking looks at five factors that can affect the value of an eSIM before, during and after a trip. Best value eSIM 2026: Overall results To determine the best eSIM for travel in 2026, the analysis compared Holafly, Saily and Airalo across five areas: Pricing Efficiency (35 percent), Included Benefits (25 percent), Customer Experience (15 percent), Travel Flexibility (15 percent) and Connection Readiness (10 percent). Holafly achieved the highest overall score at 91.1/100, ahead of Saily (86.7) and Airalo (78.6). The results show that network quality has become largely comparable across leading providers, meaning the important differences now come from real trip costs, included features, customer experience and flexibility. Which travel eSIM offers the best value for money? Price is often the first thing travelers compare, but the cheapest advertised plan is not always the cheapest option for the trip they are actually taking. Pricing Efficiency accounts for 35 percent of the overall score, making it the most heavily weighted category in the index. Instead of comparing headline prices, the analysis calculates the real trip cost for journeys lasting between 1 and 30 days, based on the plans available from each provider. Because fixed duration plans can make travelers pay for more days than they need, a plan may look cheaper at first, but the final cost can be higher once you account for the days that go unused.   Airalo and Saily require travelers to buy a 15 day plan for an 11 day trip. That means paying for four days of mobile service they do not need. By contrast, Holafly lets travelers buy exactly the number of days they need, eliminating unnecessary spending. The same pattern appeared across the trip durations analyzed between 1 and 30 days. By reflecting consistently lower real trip costs across the benchmark, Holafly achieved the highest Pricing Efficiency score at 100/100, while Saily scored 96.3 and Airalo 91.6. This was calculated by giving a 100 to the cheapest overall provider, while competitors lose points based on the exact percentage their plans cost extra. For instance, because Airalo's median costs were 8.4 percent higher than the baseline, its final score was reduced to 91.6. Paying only for the days you actually use can help keep travel costs down, but your experience abroad also depends on the extra tools that your plan has to offer. Which travel eSIM includes the most features? Price is only one part of the best value for money eSIM equation; features matter too, especially when they are included in the plan. Many travel eSIM providers advertise similar prices and unlimited data, but the experience can differ depending on what else comes with the plan at no extra cost. The benefits category compared eight features commonly used by international travelers, including hotspot sharing, regional and global plans, top ups, security tools and emergency internet access. Providers received higher scores when these features were included as standard rather than charging extra. Both Holafly and Saily achieved the maximum score of 100, but they offer different features. Holafly is the only provider to include Always On, which gives travelers complimentary backup data if they lose access to their main plan. Saily includes an integrated VPN, while Airalo scored 83.3 because fewer features are included as standard. These features can make a difference during a trip, but when plans change or something goes wrong, the support and policies behind the purchase matter too. Which travel eSIM offers the best customer experience? The experience of using a travel eSIM doesn't end after checkout: when travel plans change or problems arise during a trip, customer support and post-purchase policies can make a significant difference. To evaluate how efficiently each provider responds in these scenarios, the Customer Experience category combines verified Trustpilot ratings with the refund policy offered by each provider. While Holafly and Saily share the same Trustpilot rating of 4.7/5, their refund policies are very different: Holafly offers eligible customers up to 180 days to request a refund, compared with 30 days for Saily and 14 days for Airalo. This combination of customer satisfaction and a longer refund window gave Holafly the highest Customer Experience score at 90.75, ahead of Saily at 69.95 and Airalo at 54.45. If your trip gets cancelled, generous refund terms protect you. But in a normal scenario, another advantage relies on how easily a plan fits your actual schedule. Which travel eSIM gives travelers the most flexibility? Travelers plan their trips differently: some know exactly how long they will be away and want to pay only for those days, while others may extend their stay and need more mobile data once they are already abroad. That makes flexibility an important part of the overall value of a travel eSIM. To evaluate this, the Travel Flexibility category looked at two factors: whether travelers can buy a plan that matches the exact length of their trip, and whether they can extend an active plan without purchasing a new eSIM. Providers here take two different approaches to flexibility. Holafly lets travelers customise their plan from 1 to 90 days, ensuring they pay only for the exact duration of their trip, while Saily and Airalo sell plans in fixed blocks but allow users to extend an active plan without buying a new eSIM. As a result, all three providers achieved a score of 50 in this category, each offering flexibility at a different stage of the customer journey. Holafly offers the best value eSIM before the trip begins, while Saily and Airalo offer it once the trip is already underway. With all these options and commercial terms varying significantly across brands, travelers might question whether the underlying mobile service itself differs just as much. Is there really any difference in network quality? Network quality is often one of the first things travelers look for when comparing providers. Fast activation, reliable coverage and access to 5G networks all matter. However, the differences between leading providers are much smaller than many travelers expect. For this Connection Readiness category, the Index compares destination coverage, activation speed, multi-network support and 5G availability. The benchmark found no meaningful difference between the three providers in this category. All achieved the maximum score, reflecting comparable destination coverage, instant activation, multi-network support and 5G availability. This finding suggests that network quality is no longer the main differentiator among leading travel eSIM providers; the biggest differences come from real trip costs, included features, customer experience and travel flexibility, which account for 90 percent of the overall ranking. So, which travel eSIM is the most convenient? Choosing a travel eSIM involves more than finding the lowest advertised price: as leading providers offer similar access to mobile networks, the differences that matter most are how much you actually pay, what is included in your plan and how you are supported if something goes wrong. The Travel eSIM Value Index 2026 evaluated the five areas that influence that experience: Pricing Efficiency, Included Benefits, Customer Experience, Travel Flexibility and Connection Readiness. Together, they show how much travelers actually pay and how well a provider adapts to different trips. Based on the combined results, Holafly achieved the highest overall score, positioning it as the best value for money eSIM in 2026 with 91.1/100, followed by Saily at 86.7 and Airalo at 78.6. Holafly ranked first thanks to its combination of the lowest real-trip cost, included features, highest Customer Experience score, and flexible trip durations. The best travel eSIM is not necessarily the one with the lowest advertised price on a website. It is the one that lets you pay for the days you need, gives you useful features as part of the plan and offers support when you need it. Content provided by Holafly - Travel eSIM Value Index 2026

articles.text: ON CALL Welcome to another Friday and therefore to a fresh instalment of On Call, our weekly reader-contributed column that shares your tech support stories. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Roy” who toiled at a company that did work related to tissue donations and organ transplants. “The on-call duties were a bit hair-raising due to the high stakes involved,” Roy told On Call. “Thankfully, things typically ran well and I didn’t get too many calls in the off hours.” One call stuck in Roy’s mind, because it involved “an irate lab worker who was having difficulties logging into her workstation so she could get to work.” Roy started with the usual troubleshooting questions: was the machine connected to the network; were any lights on, and so on. “She was getting a bit more defensive, so I just reset her password and then had her change it to one she knew for sure, so we could move on with things,” he explained. Strangely, even the new password didn’t work. Roy therefore asked if the lab worker would spell the password out to him, so he could use her credentials in the company’s webmail service. The lab worker agreed and started to spell out her password. “Capital C, capital A, capital T,” she started, and then added “Capital Two.” “The last one stood out to me as a number I wasn’t so familiar with,” Roy dryly told On Call. “What’s a capital Two?” he asked. “Did you mean an ‘@’ sign?” The next thing Roy heard was the sound of his user typing. “’OK, I got it,’ she replied, before ending the call.” Have your users used confusingly odd terms to describe the everyday? If so, show your mastery of the @ symbol by sending email to Oncall@theregister.com. All donations of great stories welcome and we hope to transplant your contribution into a future edition of On Call! ®

articles.title: Google engineer unplugged every fiber they could see and – surprise! – took down a chunk of the G-Cloud
articles.text: Google Cloud has revealed the embarrassing reason for a partial outage at its us-central1-b region this week: An engineer unplugged it. The incident spanned 07:41 to 11:52 PT on September 1, and saw a portion of the G-Cloud region experience “severe network degradation and resource isolation.” “Traffic flow drop rates for resources hosted in the affected area reached 100% during the peak of the incident, resulting in unreachable virtual machines and elevated packet loss,” states Google’s service health report. The preliminary root cause on that page explains that Google designs its cloudy datacenters so they have “redundancy across multiple routing devices.” “The system is designed to be resilient to all single device or fiber-path failures, and most double-or triple-failures do not affect customer traffic. To ensure this, the devices and fiber paths are physically separated in each datacenter, with diverse power sources,” the document explains. But it’s possible to defeat all that redundancy by pulling out all the cables. “The immediate technical trigger for this event was the inadvertent physical disconnection of network fiber-optic cables during a routine hardware maintenance procedure,” Google explained. “A procedural error meant that the physical maintenance action sequentially unplugged 100% of fiber paths across all devices within 13 minutes. The nature of the error, combined with the speed of the action, prevented warnings of incorrect action reaching the engineer before complete disconnection.” Once the engineer disconnected the routers, VMs in one zone of the us-central1-b region lost contact with the outside world. They could at least chat with each other, but users couldn’t contact their VMs to figure out what was going on. Once Google noticed the situation, it moved traffic away from the routers that the engineer disconnected. At that point its resilience provisions kicked in as traffic automatically shifted what the company described as “healthy capacity elsewhere in the region.” While that was going on, technicians “identified the disconnected optical links and physically reseated the fibers. Once the physical links were fully restored, traffic flow rates normalized and the traffic was redirected back to return the capacity to service.” To summarize: A Google Cloud zone went offline because one of the company’s engineers pulled out all the cables that connected it to the internet. Once someone plugged everything in again, it started working. The Register understands that outfits like Google create detailed procedures for how to safely maintain their infrastructure, and that technicians should always follow them carefully. It therefore seems like the engineer who pulled the cables failed to observe one of the most basic rules of tech: RTFM. ®

articles.title: The search company that plants trees just launched a Linux browser to help Europe battle big tech
articles.text: Berlin-based eco-conscious search outfit Ecosia is expanding its range of European-focused web browsers to include a Linux version, citing the growing number of users in the EU looking for open alternatives to the clutches of American tech giants. Calling Linux users a “critical tech community that has long called for data privacy, digital sovereignty, and sustainability,” Ecosia said it was launching the new browser to support the community, whose numbers it says doubled in the EU between 2024 and 2025. The absolute share remains small, mind you - from 2.5 percent of EU computer users to 5.7 percent in the course of a year, but it’s still an increase that the Linux community can be proud of. Ecosia noted that Windows’ share of the market fell during that same period, from 80.2 percent to 74.2 percent. As of this writing, Linux’s share of the European desktop and console market is 6.4 percent, while Windows has dropped to 68.62 percent, per Statcounter. “Linux in particular is becoming increasingly popular among tech circles, developers, and privacy-conscious users - a target group that views commercial tech giants like Microsoft and Google with increasing skepticism,” Ecosia said. Europeans don't appear completely disillusioned with American tech, however, as macOS's share in the region has nearly doubled since August 2025. Regardless, the company said, it wants to meet Linux users where they’re at with a version of the company’s Chromium-based browser designed for trailblazing European digital sovereignty leaders freed from the grasp of Google. “With our Linux version, we're finally giving them a search engine that matches their values - climate- and privacy-friendly, and free of tech-bro monopolies," said Ecosia founder and CEO Christian Kroll. Ecosia has leaned hard into the European movement for sovereign technology in light of frustration with American tech giants, citing both the European Commission’s decision this year to require Google to share anonymized search data with eligible rival search engines, and what it says is growing dissatisfaction among Europeans over Google’s dominance of the search and browser markets. Separating the EU from Google isn’t a new initiative, with Ecosia and French search firm Qwant partnering on an EU-based web index that launched last year. It’s not clear whether that initiative has yet benefited from the EC’s order to Google to hand over search data. The duo’s initiative, the European Search Perspective (EUSP), is currently working to expand its presence to other EU languages to “lay the foundation for genuine European digital sovereignty,” though it’s not clear from the press release how far along the initiative is. Ecosia’s Linux browser is now available through the App Center on Ubuntu and directly through the Snap store. Ecosia also has browsers available for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, all of which can be downloaded by following the link on its website. While based on open-source Chromium, Ecosia's browsers themselves are not open source. We reached out to learn whether it'd be different for the Linux variant, but didn't immediately hear back. ®

articles.title: Cisco searched for IOS XR bugs and found so many it rolled them into an update release
articles.text: Cisco has warned its customers of three critical-rated flaws in its products. Two of them are present in the Cisco IOS XR operating system that powers the company’s carrier-grade kit. CVE-2026-20274 scores 9.8 on the ten-point CVSS scale and covers a buffet of buffering issues, the potential for out-of-bounds writes, and the chance to initialize resources with an insecure default. CVE-2026-20279 is another 9.8-rated flaw. Cisco says it’s an improper access control problem that covers “improper certificate validation, missing authentication for critical function, missing authorization, and incorrect authorization.” Cisco also spotted a trio of 8.8-rated flaws, plus another rated 8.6 and one more scored at 8.2 The company’s advisory says the company found the flaws after “a comprehensive internal security review,” language that perhaps hints at Cisco dabbling with Mythos and/or other bug-finding models. The fix is in: Cisco has published new versions of IOS XR that fix the problems and “strongly recommends” customers adopt them. Cisco’s support organization spotted the third critical flaw it revealed on Wednesday. CVE-2026-20212 is a tad embarrassing because the cause is a bad integration with Cisco’s own Silicon One networking processors that means some Nexus 9000 Series Switches “could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to execute code with root privileges.” “This vulnerability exists because TCP ports 43210 and 43211 are accessible in the default Layer 3 (L3) virtual routing and forwarding (VRF),” according to Cisco’s advisory. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to connect to an affected device and send crafted input that could be executed as code with root privileges. The exploitation of this vulnerability could also cause the S1HAL process to crash, which could cause the device to reload.” Ten Nexus 9000 devices have the problem, which Cisco suggests owners mitigate by using infrastructure access control lists (iACLs) to allow only required management and control plane traffic that is destined to the affected device. “Alternatively, the iACLs may be used to explicitly deny all TCP packets that are destined to a locally configured IP address with a destination port of 43210 or 43211,” the company advises. The networking giant suggests that approach because it hasn’t yet created a software update to fix the flaw once and for all. The company has, however, delivered a download that helps to implement the mitigation. Cisco hasn't seen attacks on these flaws. That may change, fast, now that evildoers can use AI to whip up nastyware. ®
